title: Where faithful Christians differ, fairly
for: I want to understand the other side
subtitle: Eight short sessions on the questions that divide faithful churches, from baptism and the Supper to predestination and the end times, each view stated in its strongest voice.
intro: Christians who confess the same creed still worship in different churches, and the reasons are not trivial. This track takes the questions that divide faithful Christians, baptism, the Lord's Supper, church government, women in office, predestination, the end times and the great traditions themselves, and lets each side speak in its strongest voice.

It will not tell you who is right on any of them. These are questions that shape how a church lives, and Christians who answer them differently still share one Lord and one faith. The pastor behind this site leads a Baptist church, and each session says so, so that you can weigh what you read. The aim is that you finish able to state the other side so well its own people would thank you.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Where faithful Christians differ, fairly. The group suits believers who want to understand Christians on the other side of a question, families and churches where two traditions meet, and outsiders puzzled by the number of churches. The leader's task is to make sure every view is heard at its strongest and that no session ends with a verdict on a question the creeds leave open.

Each person reads the session, opens its page and does what it asks before the group meets. The meeting doesn't repeat the teaching. It talks over what people found, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, and a group drawn from more than one church is a gift here. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week or once a fortnight, for eight meetings, and keep the end time you promised. A leader doesn't need to have settled these questions. A leader needs to be able to state a view they don't hold without a trace of scorn.

sections.title: The room
body: A table works best, with Bibles open in front of everyone and the session's page at hand. Say at the first meeting that the group will disagree, that this is allowed, and that the aim is understanding, not winning. Anyone may pass on any question, and no one has to pray aloud. What people say about their own churches and families stays in the room, unless someone is in danger.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Ten minutes: one person reads the verse aloud, and the passage around it, while the others follow.
Fifteen minutes: two people each state one view at its strongest, ideally a view they do not hold, and the group says whether its defenders would sign it.
Twenty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is found, in Scripture or on the page.
Ten minutes: the prayer prompt, in the group's own words, praying for Christians on the other side of the question.
Five minutes: name the next session and the page it opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: On these questions someone will want a verdict, and the track will not give one. When the room grows heated, ask first what order the question is, then ask the person arguing to state the other view until its defenders would accept it. Point to the pages the sessions open, which set out every view in its own voice. If someone from another tradition is in the group, let them explain their own church's view, and thank them for it.

Hold the line where the creeds hold it. The Trinity, the person of Christ, the resurrection and salvation by grace are not up for debate in this track, and every tradition in it confesses them. Everything else gets room.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: These questions are rarely only theory. Someone may have been refused communion, told their gift had no place, or frightened about whether they were chosen. Someone may carry a family split over a baptism. When the study touches a wound, stop and listen. Thank them for saying it, don't argue the doctrine at them, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

If someone says that a leader, a partner or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret. A child who may be in danger is a matter for the authorities, not only for the group.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home or in a church, grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: First things, second things, open questions
teaching: Not every disagreement among Christians weighs the same. A useful habit, sometimes called theological triage, sorts questions into three orders. First-order questions are those the gospel stands or falls on and the creeds bind: the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, his bodily resurrection, salvation by grace. Second-order questions divide faithful churches but not the faith, because a church has to choose one practice: baptism, the Supper, how it is governed, who may hold office. Third-order questions are open, and Christians who differ on them can share a pew in peace.

The sorting matters because two errors are always close. One treats every conviction as first-order and turns brothers and sisters into enemies. The other treats everything as open and is left with nothing to confess. The sessions that follow are all second- or third-order, so none of them lands a verdict. Each sets out the views as their own defenders would, and each names one more thing so you can allow for it: this site is written by a Baptist pastor. The test of every session is whether someone on the other side would finish it feeling understood.

sessions.question: What disagreement among Christians have you treated as more important, or less important, than it really is?
sessions.do: Open the comparison page and pick one doctrine. Read every position's best case, and write one sentence about the view you find least persuasive that its own defenders would sign.

verse.text: There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.

group.open: What is the first disagreement between churches you remember noticing?
discuss: What belongs in the first order, and how do the creeds help draw that line?
Which error are you more drawn to: treating everything as essential, or treating nothing as essential?
What would it take to state a view you disagree with so well that its defenders would thank you?
group.pray: Give thanks for the faith all Christians share, and pray for humility in the places where the group differs.

sessions.title: Baptism: infants and believers
teaching: Every church baptizes, and they agree on more than they often think. Baptism is commanded by Christ, done with water in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, and joins a person to Christ and his people. They differ on who should be baptized. Churches that baptize infants, Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist among them, read baptism as the sign of God's covenant promise, given to the children of believers as circumcision was given in Israel. They point to whole households baptized in Acts, and to the church's practice since at least the early third century.

Churches that baptize believers, Baptists and many free churches, read baptism as the sign of faith already given, a believer's public union with Christ: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27). They note that every baptism the New Testament describes in detail follows repentance and faith. Each side has strong texts and reads the other's carefully. This site's author is a Baptist pastor, and Baptist churches baptize believers; that is named so you can weigh what you read, not to settle the question. Faithful Christians stand on both sides of it.

open.label: Babies or believers? Why Christians baptize differently
open.why: An essay that sets out both practices at their strongest, their history and their texts, and leaves the question with the reader.

sessions.question: What is the strongest argument for the view of baptism you do not hold?
sessions.do: Read the essay to the end, then read Acts 16:25-34 and Romans 6:1-11. Write the best case each side would make from those two passages.

verse.text: For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.

group.open: Were you baptized, and if so, how old were you and what do you remember?
discuss: What do churches that baptize infants and churches that baptize believers agree on about baptism?
Which texts carry the most weight for each side, and how does the other side read them?
How should a family or a church handle this question when two traditions meet under one roof?
group.pray: Give thanks for baptism, and pray for Christians on both sides of this question, that they would honor one another.

sessions.title: The Lord's Supper
teaching: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and a cup and told his friends to do this in remembrance of him. Every church obeys, and every church believes the meal matters. They differ on what happens at it. Catholics hold transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ in their substance, while their appearance remains. The Orthodox confess a real change and decline to define how it happens. Lutherans hold that Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine.

The Reformed tradition, following Calvin, teaches a real spiritual presence: by the Spirit, believers truly feed on Christ, who is in heaven. Zwingli and many free churches stress the meal as a memorial and a proclamation, a remembering that is itself an act of faith. Paul's question sits under all of them: “And is not the bread that we break a participation in the body of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 10:16). The author of this site is a Baptist pastor. Many Baptists hold the memorial view, and the 1689 Baptist Confession teaches a spiritual feeding much like Calvin's. Neither is argued for here.

sessions.question: What do you believe happens when Christians eat the Lord's Supper, and where did you learn it?
sessions.do: Read 1 Corinthians 11:17-34 and John 6:47-58. Note which words each view of the Supper leans on most, and how the others read them.

verse.text: Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf.

group.open: What is your earliest memory of communion, or of being left out of it?
discuss: What do all the views of the Supper agree on?
What would a Catholic, a Lutheran, a Reformed Christian and a Baptist each most want you to understand about their view?
Why do Christians who confess one Lord still often eat at separate tables, and what does that cost?
group.pray: Give thanks for the Lord's Supper, and pray for the day when Christians now divided will eat at one table.

sessions.title: How a church is governed
teaching: Every church is governed by someone, and the New Testament shows apostles, elders and deacons, a council at Jerusalem, and congregations choosing their own servants. Three main patterns grew from those texts. Episcopal churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and some Methodist, are led by bishops in succession from the apostles, with priests and deacons under them. They see in the bishop a living link to the apostles and a guard of the church's unity. Presbyterian and Reformed churches are governed by elders, teaching and ruling, gathered in regional assemblies, and they read elder and overseer as one office.

Congregational churches, Baptists among them, place final authority under Christ in the gathered local church, led by pastors and deacons and accountable to the members. They point to whole churches choosing and correcting in Acts and the letters. This site's author pastors a Baptist church, governed in this way; the session does not argue for it. Each pattern has a typical danger: bishops can grow distant, elders can become a closed circle, and a congregation can become a popular vote. Scripture asks the same of all of them: leaders who serve, who answer to others, and who do not lord it over the flock.

sessions.question: What does a church need most from its leaders, whatever its form of government?
sessions.do: Read Acts 6:1-7, Acts 15:1-29 and 1 Peter 5:1-5. Note who decides in each passage, and how each tradition might read it.

verse.text: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock.

care: If you have been harmed by a controlling leader or church, what was done was wrong, and it was not your fault. You are free to step away and to tell someone you trust. If you were abused in other ways, or a crime was done, it should be reported to the authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Who made the big decisions in the churches you have known?
discuss: What strength does each pattern, bishops, elders or congregations, protect, and what danger does each face?
Which texts would the defenders of each pattern point to first?
How can a church of any form keep its leaders accountable and its members cared for?
group.pray: Pray for the leaders of your church by name, that they would serve rather than rule, and for anyone who has been harmed by a leader.

sessions.title: Women in church office
teaching: Few questions divide churches as quickly. Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and both bear God's image, and that Scripture reserves the office of pastor or elder to qualified men. Their strongest case rests on Paul's instruction in 1 Timothy 2 and 3, which he grounds not in local custom but in the order of creation, and on the pattern of male elders across the New Testament. They insist that women's gifts be used everywhere else, and that the limit says nothing about worth.

Egalitarians hold that the same Spirit who gives gifts to both sexes opens every office to both. Their strongest case rests on the women the New Testament names in ministry: Phoebe the deacon, Junia, whom many read as counted among the apostles, Priscilla teaching Apollos, and daughters who prophesy. They read 1 Timothy 2 as answering a particular problem in Ephesus. Both sides got where they are by reading Paul. Baptists are divided on this too, and this site's author is a Baptist pastor; that is said so you can weigh it, and the session takes no side. The creeds are silent. A church still has to decide who preaches on Sunday.

open.why: An essay that sets the complementarian and egalitarian readings side by side, at their strongest, and leaves the conclusion to the reader and the reader's church.

sessions.question: What is the strongest case for the view on women in office that you do not hold?
sessions.do: Read 1 Timothy 2:8-15 and Romans 16:1-16. For each passage, write how a complementarian and an egalitarian would read it at their best.

verse.text: As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another.

group.open: What have you seen women do in the churches you have known?
discuss: What would a thoughtful complementarian most want you to understand about that view?
What would a thoughtful egalitarian most want you to understand about that view?
Whatever a church concludes, how can it make sure the women in it are taught, heard and given room to use their gifts?
group.pray: Pray for the women and men of your church to use every gift God has given them, and for unity across this disagreement.

sessions.title: Predestination and free will
teaching: Scripture says both that God chooses and that people must choose. Paul writes of those God “predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son” (Romans 8:29), and the same Bible calls everyone everywhere to repent and believe. Calvinists, following Augustine and the Reformed confessions, hold that God chose some for salvation unconditionally, and that his grace given to them will surely bring them to faith. They point to Romans 9 and John 6, and say the doctrine leaves no room for boasting and gives the believer deep security.

Arminians, following Jacob Arminius and John Wesley, hold that God's grace goes before every person, enabling a free response that can be refused, and that God chose those he foresaw would believe. They point to texts where God desires all people to be saved, and say only this keeps God's love universal and human response real. Many hold neither system whole. Baptists have stood on both sides from the beginning, and this site's author is a Baptist pastor; no side is argued here. Both views confess salvation by grace. And Paul, at the end of his own argument, stopped explaining and worshiped.

open.why: Calvinism, Arminianism and the traditionalist view held by many Baptists, each stated by its own best defenders, with their key texts.

also.label: How can God be sovereign and humans still be free?

also.label: Did God choose who would be saved?

also.label: Does God choose us, or do we choose him?
also.why: The Honest Answer for the reader troubled by this question, with each tradition's view stated fairly.

sessions.question: Which do you find harder to accept, that God chooses or that people truly choose, and why?
sessions.do: Read Romans 9:1-24 and 1 Timothy 2:1-6 together. Write the best case each side would make from the passage it finds harder.

verse.text: O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!

care: If you are afraid that you are not chosen, hear the invitation of Jesus: “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37). That fear is not usually the mark of someone God has turned away. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: Have you ever worried about whether you were chosen, or whether you had chosen well enough?
discuss: What does each view protect that its defenders would never give up?
How do Calvinists and Arminians each read the texts the other side finds strongest?
Why do you think Paul ended Romans 9 to 11 in worship rather than in a solution?
group.pray: Pray for anyone troubled by this question, and give thanks that salvation rests on God's grace however it is answered.

sessions.title: The millennium and the end times
teaching: Revelation 20 speaks of a thousand years in which Satan is bound and the faithful reign with Christ, and Christians have read it in four main ways. Amillennialists read the thousand years as a picture of the present age, with Christ reigning from heaven between his two comings. Postmillennialists expect the gospel to bring the nations broadly under Christ's rule before he returns. Historic premillennialists expect Christ to return before an earthly reign, with the church passing through the final tribulation. Dispensational premillennialists add a rapture of the church and a distinct future for national Israel.

Each view has had great defenders. Augustine's reading shaped the amillennial view for centuries, postmillennial hope helped drive the modern missionary movement, and premillennialism was held by early writers like Irenaeus and revived among modern evangelicals. This is third-order: the creeds bind the return of Christ and the judgment, not the shape of Revelation 20. Baptists hold all four views, and this site's author, a Baptist pastor, argues for none of them here. Every generation has been tempted to read its news into Revelation. The book was written to make a suffering church faithful, not anxious.

sessions.do: Read Revelation 20 slowly, then the guide to reading apocalyptic. Write one sentence for each of the four views on how it reads verse 4.

verse.text: He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

discuss: What does each of the four views do with Revelation 20?
Why might the creeds bind Christ's return but leave the millennium open?
How can Christians who differ here still share the same hope?
group.pray: Pray for persecuted Christians today, and ask for a hope in Christ's return that makes the group faithful rather than anxious.

sessions.title: The great traditions, in their own words
teaching: Most Christians in the world belong to one of three great families. The Orthodox would want you to know they are not Catholics without a pope. They see themselves as the church of the councils, keeping the faith whole through worship, icons and the hope that people may share in God's own life. Catholics would want you to know that they believe salvation is by grace, and that the one visible church, with its sacraments and teaching office, is how Christ keeps his people together. East and West divided in 1054, and the wound has never closed.

Protestants, born in the Reformation that began in 1517, would want you to know they meant not to start a new church but to call the old one back to Scripture, to grace received by faith, and to the priesthood of all believers. Baptists are Protestants of the free-church kind, and this site's author is one; no family is argued for here. Each confesses the creeds, and each names real failures in the others. Jesus prayed that his people would be one so that the world would believe. That prayer has not yet been answered in a way the world can see, and every divided table is set in the meantime.

sessions.question: Which of the three great traditions do you understand least, and what would you need to understand it better?
sessions.do: Read the traditions page on the family you know least. Write three sentences describing it as one of its own members would, and if you can, ask one of them whether you got it right.

verse.text: that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You. May they also be in Us, so that the world may believe that You sent Me.

group.open: Have you ever worshiped in a tradition other than your own? What did you notice?
discuss: What would an Orthodox, a Catholic and a Protestant Christian each most want you to understand about their church?
What does every great tradition share, according to the creeds?
What would it look like to hold your own convictions and still pray honestly for the unity Christ prayed for?
group.pray: Pray for Christians of every tradition, by name where you know them, and for the unity Christ prayed for.
